name: Pub Street Khmer Kitchen
nameKm: ផ្ទះបាយខ្មែរផាប់ស្ទ្រីត
shortDescription: A busy two-floor Khmer restaurant one lane off Pub Street, serving amok, lok lak and the curries most visitors are looking for, done properly, with a balcony over the crowd.
description: Pub Street Khmer Kitchen opened in 2013 to feed the temple crowds something better than the street's fried-rice standard. The menu is the Khmer classics cooked with care: fish amok steamed in banana leaf until it just sets, beef lok lak with a sharp lime-and-pepper dip, a green Kampot pepper stir-fry of squid, samlor korko vegetable soup and, for the brave, beef with red tree ants. Portions are generous and the spice is honest but adjustable. The ground floor is loud and quick; the first-floor balcony is where to sit with a jug of Angkor draught and watch Pub Street fill up. English, Khmer and Chinese menus with pictures make ordering easy.

nameKm: គុយទាវពេលព្រឹកអង្គរ
shortDescription: A dawn kuy teav cart on the road out to the temples, ladling pork-bone broth over rice noodles for drivers, guides and anyone heading for sunrise who was smart enough to stop.
description: Mrs Sophal has pushed her noodle cart to the same corner on the Angkor road since 2009, and by half past five the plastic stools are full of tuk-tuk drivers waiting for their sunrise passengers. The dish is kuy teav: rice noodles in a clear pork-bone broth simmered overnight, topped with sliced pork, a few prawns, minced pork, bean sprouts, fried garlic and a squeeze of lime, with chilli, pickled chilli and fish sauce on the table to finish it yourself. There is also a dry version with the broth on the side. She is sold out by ten. Pull up on the way to the temples and eat what the drivers eat.

name: Kandal Village Café
nameKm: ហាងកាហ្វេកណ្ដាលវីលេជ
shortDescription: A bright shophouse café in Kandal Village with single-origin Cambodian coffee, a brunch menu of eggs, sourdough and Khmer-leaning plates, and a courtyard that stays cool until noon.
description: Kandal Village Café was one of the first to open in the lane of boutiques and galleries north of the Old Market, in 2015, and it still sets the standard for a Siem Reap brunch. The coffee is roasted in Phnom Penh from Mondulkiri beans and pulled on a proper machine, with cold brew and oat milk for those who want them. The food runs from eggs on sourdough and granola to a Khmer breakfast of bai sach chrouk and a very good pumpkin and coconut soup. The room is white tile and old timber with a shaded courtyard behind, the wifi is quick, and laptops are tolerated until the lunch rush.

nameKm: ផ្ទះត្រីទន្លេសាប
shortDescription: A family restaurant on the road to the lake that cooks Tonle Sap fish the way lake families do: amok, sour soup, grilled snakehead and fried fish with green mango, under a tin roof with fans.
description: Tonlé Sap Fish House is a big open-sided restaurant on the road south towards Chong Kneas, run by a family who came off the lake a generation ago and still buy from the boats each morning. The fish amok here is the real thing, thick with fresh kroeung and coconut cream and steamed in banana leaf; alongside it come samlor machu, the sour fish soup with tamarind and lotus stem, whole snakehead grilled over charcoal with a dip of lime and salt, and crisp fried fish with a shredded green mango salad. The tin roof and ceiling fans keep it cool enough, and prices are low. Go with several people and order for the table.

name: Old Market Smoothie Bar
nameKm: ហាងទឹកផ្លែឈើផ្សារចាស់
shortDescription: A hole-in-the-wall juice counter on the Old Market corner, blending mango, passion fruit, dragon fruit and coconut to order for a dollar or two, open from breakfast until the bars fill.
description: Old Market Smoothie Bar is a counter three metres wide on the corner facing Psar Chas, with a wall of fruit stacked behind it and a row of blenders that rarely stop. Everything is made to order from what came in from the market that morning: mango, passion fruit, dragon fruit, pineapple, soursop and banana, blended with ice and a little palm sugar or with coconut water and nothing else. Young coconuts are opened with a cleaver while you wait, and a few stools let you drink it on the spot. It has been run by the same two sisters since 2014 and is the sensible stop between the market and the night market.

nameKm: នំបញ្ចុកព្រះដាក់
shortDescription: The best-known of the noodle stalls in Preah Dak village on the Banteay Srei road, pressing fresh rice noodles each morning and serving them under green fish gravy with a heap of herbs.
description: Preah Dak, the village on the road to Banteay Srei, has been known for num banh chok for generations, and the stall of Yeay Phan, run by her daughters since 2010, is the one the drivers pull in at. The noodles are pressed fresh each dawn from fermented rice, soft and slightly sour, and ladled with a thin green gravy of fish, lemongrass, turmeric and galangal, or a red one with coconut and chilli for those who ask. On top goes whatever is fresh: banana blossom, cucumber, water lily stem, long beans, mint and sweet basil. A bowl costs a dollar. They also sell num kroch and sticky-rice sweets to take to the temple.

shortDescription: A sprawling evening barbecue hall two streets off the quay, with charcoal braziers at every table, marinated beef, pork and seafood by the plate, and jugs of draught beer until late.
description: Riverside Grill House is Phnom Penh's barbecue tradition done at scale: a hundred-seat hall open to the street, each table fitted with a charcoal brazier and a domed grill that cooks meat on top and simmers broth in the moat around it. You order by the plate: beef in lemongrass marinade, pork belly, squid, prawns, mushrooms and morning glory for the soup, with dips of lime, pepper and prahok on the side. Draught Angkor comes in jugs with ice, the music is loud and local, and by nine every table is full of families and office groups celebrating something. Prices are low, the smoke is part of the deal, and you will smell of it until morning.

nameKm: តាប៉ាសច្រកបាសាក់
shortDescription: A narrow bar-restaurant in the Bassac Lane alley doing Khmer-inflected small plates, natural wines and cocktails built on local spirits, with a counter kitchen and a courtyard at the back.
description: Bassac Lane Tapas took over a shophouse in the alley of bars behind Street 308 in 2019 and gave it a kitchen worth sitting at. The plates are small and meant for sharing: Kampot pepper squid, pork belly glazed with palm sugar, a prahok ktis dip with raw vegetables, and grilled river prawns with green mango. The bar pours natural wines by the glass and cocktails built on Cambodian rice spirit, Kampot pepper and tamarind, with a happy hour from five to seven. Inside is twenty stools along a counter and the open kitchen; behind, a courtyard under a tamarind tree. Book for Friday and Saturday, when the alley is at its busiest and the kitchen runs until one.

shortDescription: The breakfast stalls on the ground floor of Orussey Market, where Phnom Penh eats bai sach chrouk, kuy teav and rice porridge from five in the morning on shared steel tables.
description: Orussey Market, a few blocks west of the Central Market, is the capital's wholesale market for everything from dried fish to school shoes, and its ground-floor food hall is where the market workers and half the neighbourhood eat breakfast. Twenty or so stalls share the long steel tables. The thing to order is bai sach chrouk: thin slices of pork marinated in coconut milk and garlic, grilled over charcoal before dawn and served over broken rice with pickled cucumber and daikon and a bowl of clear broth. Kuy teav, rice porridge and iced coffee are at the stalls alongside. It is over by eleven. Go early, point, and sit where there is room.

nameKm: កាហ្វេទួលទំពូង
shortDescription: A small roastery café behind the Russian Market that roasts Mondulkiri and Ratanakiri beans on site, pours them as espresso, pour-over and cold brew, and sells bags by the kilo.
description: Toul Tom Poung Coffee is a roastery first and a café second, opened in 2017 in a shophouse two streets from the Russian Market by a couple who spent years buying cherries from Bunong farmers around Sen Monorom. The roaster sits in the window and runs most mornings. The menu is short: espresso drinks, pour-over of whichever single-origin lot is on, a slow-drip Khmer iced coffee with condensed milk for tradition, and cold brew in bottles for the heat. Food is a few pastries from a neighbour's bakery. Beans go out by the kilo to half the cafés in the quarter and in bags to visitors, and a cupping is held on Saturday mornings.

name: Royal Khmer Dining
nameKm: ភោជនីយដ្ឋានខ្មែររាជវាំង
shortDescription: A formal Khmer dining room in a restored villa near the palace, reviving recipes of the royal kitchens in multi-course set menus, with a wine list to match and a garden for aperitifs.
description: Royal Khmer Dining occupies a 1930s villa on a quiet street behind the Royal Palace, restored with teak floors, silk panels and a garden of frangipani where guests take a drink before dinner. The kitchen is led by a chef who trained with elders of the palace household, and the menus revive the refined end of Khmer cooking: a seven-course tasting that moves from a banana-blossom salad with smoked fish through samlor kari with duck, Kampot lobster in green pepper and a slow-cooked beef saraman to palm-sugar custards and jasmine tea. The wine list is short and well chosen, with a pairing available. Jackets are not required but shorts are turned away, and reservations are needed most evenings.

shortDescription: A fourth-floor rooftop on the quay with the river junction in front of it, cocktails built on Khmer ingredients, a sharing menu of grills and a live band from Thursday to Saturday.
description: Sisowath Sunset Bar runs across the roof of a corner building on the quay, four floors above the promenade, with the Tonle Sap and the Mekong meeting in front of it and the palace roofs to the south. People come at half past five for the sunset and stay for the band. The cocktail list leans on local flavours, with a Kampot pepper margarita, a tamarind sour and a rice-spirit old fashioned, and the happy hour runs until seven. The kitchen does sharing plates and grills, from pepper-crusted beef skewers to grilled whole fish. A band plays from Thursday to Saturday and a DJ follows on weekends until two. Book a table at the rail.

description: Street 240 Bakery opened in 2011 on the leafy street of boutiques behind the palace, run by a Khmer baker who learned the trade in Lyon and came home. The ovens run from four in the morning and again at noon, so the baguettes are warm at breakfast and at lunch; the croissants, pain au chocolat and kouign-amann go early, the lemon and passion-fruit tarts last until afternoon. At lunch a counter of baguette sandwiches, from pâté and pickles in the Cambodian num pang style to ham and comté, serves the offices and galleries of the street, and the coffee is a Phnom Penh roast. The few tables on the pavement under the trees are the best seats.

shortDescription: A riverside shack on the Kampot waterfront that keeps its crabs live in the river and stir-fries them with fresh green pepper from the farm up the road, with cold beer and a sunset for free.
description: Kampot Pepper Crab Shack is a tin-roofed restaurant on the river just north of the Old Bridge, run by a fishing family who truck crabs from Kep every morning and keep them in baskets in the river until ordered. The signature dish is the coast's own: crab chopped and stir-fried in the wok with garlic, oyster sauce and whole strands of fresh green Kampot pepper from a farm the family part-owns. Prawns in tamarind, grilled squid with lime and salt, steamed clams with basil and a fish amok fill out the menu, and the beer is cold. Tables sit on a wooden deck over the water facing the Bokor ridge, so the sunset is part of dinner.

nameKm: អាហារតូចៗផ្សាររាត្រីកំពត
shortDescription: A grill stall at the Kampot night market, skewering pork, chicken wings and squid over charcoal from late afternoon, with a dessert cart of grilled bananas and sticky rice beside it.
description: The night market behind the Kampot riverfront fills each evening with carts, and the grill of Bong Vuthy at the river end is the one with the queue. Skewers of pork marinated in lemongrass and palm sugar, chicken wings in a sticky fish-sauce glaze, whole squid and small river fish go over the charcoal from half past four, served on paper with pickled papaya and a chilli dip for a dollar or two a skewer. His wife runs the dessert cart alongside: bananas grilled in their skins with a coconut-caramel sauce, sticky rice in bamboo, and num plae ai, the little rice-flour dumplings in coconut. Most people eat standing or carry it to the river wall.

name: Kep Crab Pier Restaurant
nameKm: ភោជនីយដ្ឋានផែក្ដាមកែប
shortDescription: One of the stilt restaurants at the Kep crab market, choosing your blue swimmer crabs live from the basket and cooking them six ways, with grilled squid, prawns and the sea under the floorboards.
description: Kep Crab Pier is the third restaurant along the row of stilt houses behind the crab market, run by the Sem family since 2008. The routine is simple: you walk to the basket in the shallows, choose your crabs, agree a price by the kilo, and they are in the wok within minutes. Green Kampot pepper is the classic, but the kitchen also does them steamed with lemongrass, in a tamarind sauce, with salted egg, in a curry and simply grilled. Prawns, squid, clams and whole fish come off the same boats. The floor is planks over the water, the breeze comes through the walls and the sunset over Rabbit Island lands on the table.

description: Kep Plantation Café sits in a garden on the road that climbs towards the national park, a shaded terrace among pepper vines, frangipani and a vegetable patch that supplies the kitchen. The coffee is from Mondulkiri and pulled on a small machine, and the house drink is a hot chocolate spiked with ground red Kampot pepper. Lunch is light: a pepper-crusted fish salad, a vegetable curry with rice, baguette sandwiches and a daily soup, followed by a passion-fruit cheesecake or a palm-sugar flan. The shop at the back sells the farm's own pepper in four colours, Kampot sea salt, palm sugar and jams, packed for luggage. Mornings are cool; the lunch crowd arrives after the trail.

shortDescription: A family stall at the bamboo train terminus cooking rice plates over a gas wok and charcoal, fried rice, stir-fried morning glory, grilled chicken and cold coconuts for riders waiting for the next car.
description: The canteen at the end of the bamboo train line is a thatched shelter with a wok, a charcoal grill and a dozen plastic tables, run by a family who farm the rice fields the train runs through. The food is what a Khmer farmhouse eats at midday: fried rice with egg and pork, morning glory stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce, grilled chicken with lime and pepper, a sour soup when there is fish, and plates of fresh pineapple and mango. Young coconuts are hacked open from a pile under the table and cost a dollar. Nothing is written down; point at what is cooking and it arrives in a few minutes, before the car turns around.

nameKm: ប៊ីស្ត្រូបេតិកភណ្ឌបាត់ដំបង
shortDescription: A bistro in a restored riverside shophouse pairing Khmer home cooking with French technique, from a duck and green-pepper confit to a prahok-and-pork dip, with Battambang's own art on the walls.
description: Battambang Heritage Bistro opened in 2017 in a 1920s shophouse on the river road, its tiles, teak staircase and shutters intact and the walls hung with paintings from the galleries next door. The kitchen is run by a Battambang chef who worked in Lyon and a sous-chef from the village, and the menu moves between the two: duck confit with green Kampot pepper, a slow beef saraman curry with baguette, fish amok done the classic way, prahok ktis with crudités, and a chocolate and palm-sugar tart. There is a short French wine list, local craft beer and Battambang rice wine infused with ginger. Lunch is a two-course set that the town's office workers favour; dinner is quieter and candlelit.

shortDescription: A beach-bar restaurant on the sand at Otres grilling the day's fish, squid and prawns over charcoal from lunch until late, with cocktails, happy hour and tables that move with the tide.
description: Otres Beach BBQ is one of the few beach bars left on the sand after the clearances, a timber-and-thatch kitchen with its tables set out on the beach and moved back as the tide comes in. The fishermen's boats land at the southern end each morning, and whatever came in goes on the display: barracuda, red snapper, squid, tiger prawns and crab, priced by weight and grilled over charcoal with a choice of garlic butter, Kampot pepper or a Khmer chilli-lime marinade, served with rice, salad and grilled vegetables. Happy hour on cocktails and draught runs from four to seven, the sunset is straight ahead, and after dark the lanterns go on and the music goes up a little.

name: Koh Rong Fisherman's Shack
nameKm: ខ្ទមអ្នកនេសាទកោះរ៉ុង
shortDescription: A fisherman's family restaurant on the Koh Touch beach path serving whatever the father's boat brought in that morning, grilled or in a Khmer sour soup, with rice, cold beer and sand underfoot.
description: Koh Rong Fisherman's Shack is exactly that: the house of a fishing family at the quieter end of Koh Touch, with a dozen tables under a thatch roof and the day's catch in a cooler by the door. The father goes out before dawn, the mother and daughters cook, and the chalkboard changes with the boat: grouper, mackerel, squid, crab and sometimes a lobster or two, grilled over coconut-husk charcoal with a lime and salt dip, fried whole with garlic, or cooked into samlor machu, the sour soup with pineapple and tomato. Rice, a green papaya salad and a vegetable stir-fry round it out. Cards do not work, and when the fish is gone the shack closes.

description: Every morning before five, Om Srey sets up her cart under the tamarind trees on the Kratie riverfront, between the Koh Trong ferry landing and the market, and lights three pots. One is kuy teav, pork-bone broth over rice noodles with sliced pork and a few prawns; one is a beef noodle soup with a dark star-anise broth; the third is bobor, rice porridge with river fish, ginger and fried garlic. Everything is served with a plate of herbs, lime, chilli and bean sprouts. Ferry workers eat first, then the market women, then the dolphin-bound travellers. By ten the pots are empty. The sun comes up over Koh Trong while you eat.

shortDescription: A roastery café on the main street of Sen Monorom that buys cherries from Bunong farms on the plateau, roasts in a drum in the back and serves the result as espresso, pour-over and Khmer iced coffee.
description: Sen Monorom Coffee Roastery is the place in town to taste the plateau's crop properly. The owners, a Bunong farmer and his Khmer wife, buy ripe cherries from a dozen neighbouring smallholders at a premium for careful picking, process them on the farm and roast in a small drum behind the counter three mornings a week. The café serves espresso and flat whites, pour-overs of single-farm lots, cold brew in the hot months and, for the locals, a strong slow-drip coffee over ice with condensed milk. Food is banana bread and sticky-rice cakes. Bags of beans go home with most visitors, and a half-day farm tour with a cupping at the end leaves at eight on request.

description: Kampong Cham Mekong Grill spreads along the riverfront under the big trees south of the bridge, a kitchen in a shophouse and forty tables outside facing the water. The fish comes off the boats at the landing beside it: trey ros, trey pra and giant snakehead, rubbed with salt, turmeric and lemongrass and grilled whole over charcoal until the skin blisters, served with a plate of herbs, rice and a tamarind dip. Alongside come pork ribs glazed with palm sugar, samlor machu sour soup with Mekong fish, grilled chicken and a morning-glory stir-fry. It has fed the town since 2009 and fills at dusk when the lights come on along the bamboo bridge to Koh Paen.

shortDescription: The dawn fish market on the lakefront in Takeo town, where boats land freshwater fish, eels and lobster from the wetlands, and the prahok stalls, grilled-fish sellers and soup pots feed the crowd that buys.
description: Takeo's lakefront market works from before dawn, when the boats come in across the wetland from Angkor Borei with the night's catch: snakehead, catfish, climbing perch, eels and the giant freshwater prawns the province is known for. Behind the fish, forty-odd stalls sell the vegetables and herbs of the floodplain, and a row of prahok sellers scoop the fermented fish paste from clay jars. Around the edge, cooks grill fish on bamboo over charcoal, simmer pots of samlor and fry up num banh chok for the buyers. Two dollars gets a grilled fish with rice, eaten on a stool by the water. The market is at its best between five and eight and winds down by noon.
